strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem statement: training diffusion/flow policies in online RL requires sampling from an unnormalized Boltzmann distribution, which standard conditional flow matching cannot handle; the paper's 'reverse inference' reframing (posterior over noise/data given the interpolant, Eq. 6-7) is elegant and well executed.

Theoretically clean framework: Proposition 1 and Theorem 1 (equivalence of RFM, noise-posterior and data-posterior forms, and conditional flow matching under mutual absolute continuity) are carefully stated and proved; the use of generalized Langevin Stein operators to build vector-valued zero-mean control variates (Defs. 1-2, Props. 2-5) is a principled and fairly novel variance-reduction construction, with closed-form optimal coefficients for the Boltzmann case (Theorem 2).

The unification in Appendix B is convincing: iDEM/DQS and QNE/RSM are shown to be exact special cases (eta = 1 vs eta = 0) of the same posterior mean estimator, which genuinely clarifies the relationship between two previously disconnected families.
Useful extension of Boltzmann-targeting objectives from diffusion to flow policies, plus a sensible extension to reverse score matching for non-Gaussian sources (Appendix A).

Empirically, the method is the only one of five tested that performs consistently across all eight DMC tasks, with 95% CIs over five seeds and baselines re-implemented in a shared codebase with identical architectures.
Writing is clear and well organized; the background section makes the paper largely self-contained.
weaknesses: Missing ablations for the central empirical claim: the paper argues that combining Q-value and Q-gradient information via the variance-minimizing Lambda (Prop. 4/5) 'improves training efficiency and stability', but there is no experiment isolating the control variate (e.g., eta = 0, eta = 1, and learned Lambda compared head-to-head), no sensitivity analysis of N (number of SNIS samples), lambda, or t_min, and no wall-clock/compute comparison showing what the added cost of gradient evaluations and weight computation buys.

Theory-practice gap not addressed: Theorem 1 assumes the proposal p_hat_t is mutually absolutely continuous with the true marginal p_t, but in the algorithm a_t is drawn by perturbing replay-buffer actions; whether this proposal satisfies the assumption (especially early in training) is not analyzed. Also, the optimal Lambda is estimated from the same samples used in the estimator (Eq. 18), a known source of finite-sample bias that is not discussed; only asymptotic variance (Lemma 3) is treated, while SNIS bias and effective sample size degradation from exp(Q/lambda) weights in higher dimensions are ignored.

Evaluation scope is narrow: only eight DMC locomotion tasks with five seeds; no harder benchmark suites (e.g., HumanoidBench, proprioceptive manipulation suites), and, notably, no comparison against existing flow-based online RL baselines (e.g., Lv et al. [18], Fan et al. [22]) despite the paper's emphasis on extending Boltzmann targeting to flow policies.

No limitations section, and no mention of code release, which hurts reproducibility given many implementation details (N, t_min, network sizes, lambda schedule) are deferred or unspecified in the main text.

Several results are relatively standard or straightforward: Lemma 2-3 and Props. 4-5 are classical control-variate/importance-sampling theory applied in a new context, and the equivalence proofs rely on standard conditional-expectation decompositions; the novelty rests mainly on the unification and the Boltzmann instantiation.

The claim that the minimum-variance estimator improves 'training efficiency and stability for both diffusion and flow policies' is only instantiated and tested for the flow case; diffusion-policy experiments with the learned Lambda are absent.

strengths: The reverse inference perspective is clean and well-motivated: reformulating flow matching without target samples as a posterior mean estimation problem (Sec. 4.1) is an appealing reframing, and Proposition 1 / Theorem 1 are stated and proved carefully.

Appendix B provides a genuinely useful service: it maps prior noise-expectation (QNE, RSM) and gradient-expectation (iDEM, DQS) methods into a single estimator family indexed by the control-variate coefficient η, with detailed schedule correspondences. This clarifies the relationship between two previously disconnected method families.

The Langevin Stein control variate construction (Def. 2, Props. 2–5) is technically sound, and the flow-policy instantiation is, to my knowledge, the first flow policy trained to target Boltzmann distributions in online RL — a real (if narrow) extension over diffusion-only prior work.
The empirical evaluation covers eight DeepMind Control Suite tasks with five seeds and a shared codebase for baselines, and the method appears consistently competitive.
weaknesses: The theoretical novelty is modest relative to the framing. Theorem 1 essentially restates the standard FM/CFM equivalence under a rich-function-class assumption, and the practical estimator reduces to SNIS with a Gaussian proposal — precisely what QNE/iDEM already do. The practical delta over prior work amounts to adding a constant-diagonal control variate with a tuned η, which is an incremental contribution dressed in general language. Proposition 3 (zero-variance condition) is a triviality, and the more expressive test-function families that would make the framework substantive are deferred to a remark (Remark 3) without any theory or experiments.

The optimal coefficient Λ* in (20) depends on the unknown posterior mean µ0|t, which is the very quantity being estimated. Estimating Λ from the same samples introduces dependence and bias in the resulting SNIS estimator, and the paper offers no analysis (bias, consistency, or even empirical variance measurement) of this circularity. The variance-reduction claims that motivate the whole framework are never actually verified empirically.

The mismatch between the proposal p̂t used to sample Xt and the true marginal pt is acknowledged (end of Theorem 1 proof) but never analyzed. In the RL instantiation, at is sampled from replay-buffer actions perturbed with noise — a distribution determined by behavior-policy coverage. Since global minimizers coincide only under mutual absolute continuity and exact minimization, the practical effect of this weighting on optimization dynamics is unexamined; this is arguably the crux of the method in the non-idealized regime.

Known practical failure modes of SNIS with exponentiated-Q weights (weight degeneracy when the Q-function range is large, especially early in training) are not discussed, nor is any mitigation (tempering, weight clipping) reported. The temperature λ and its tuning procedure are not specified.

The experimental section is thin: no ablations of the control variate (η = 0 vs η = 1 vs estimated Λ), sample count N, t_min, or the flow-vs-diffusion choice; no wall-clock/compute comparison despite N Q-gradient evaluations per actor step; and the headline claim that RFM is 'the only algorithm that performs consistently well' is not supported by statistical comparisons in several tasks where curves overlap. Baselines were reimplemented in a shared codebase, raising the possibility of weakened baselines, and no comparison to the original published numbers is given.

Reproducibility is inadequate: no code release is mentioned, and key hyperparameters (λ, N, t_min, network architectures, learning rates, replay-buffer sizes) are absent from the manuscript. There is also no limitations section, despite several substantive limitations (proposal mismatch, SNIS degeneracy, circular Λ estimation) being evident.

strengths: The paper offers a clean and well-motivated conceptual unification: the noise-expectation family (QNE/RSM) and gradient-expectation family (iDEM/DQS) are shown, with explicit derivations in Appendix B, to be special cases (η=0 and η=1) of a single posterior-mean estimation problem under reverse flow matching. This is a genuinely useful clarifying contribution for the subfield.

The reverse inferential perspective (treating X0 as latent given an observed Xt) is elegant and yields a tractable loss (9)-(10) when target samples are unavailable. The equivalence results (Proposition 1, Theorem 1, and the reverse score matching extensions in Appendix A) are stated and proved carefully.

The Langevin Stein operator construction for vector-valued zero-mean control variates (Definitions 1-2, Propositions 2-5) is a principled variance-reduction mechanism, and the optimal coefficients (20)-(21) are derived cleanly, with a sensible mapping to Boltzmann targets in Theorem 2.

Extending Boltzmann-targeted training from diffusion to flow policies fills a real gap noted in prior work, and the empirical results on eight DMC tasks show consistent performance across environments where baselines (SAC, QSM, QNE, DQS) fail on some tasks. Using a shared codebase and identical architectures improves fairness of comparison.
The writing is generally clear and well-organized; background sections are self-contained and the proofs in the main text are readable.
weaknesses: The central practical claim—that the learned optimal control variate (minimum-variance estimator) improves training efficiency and stability—is not directly validated. There are no ablations comparing RFM with η=0 (noise-expectation), η=1 (gradient-expectation), and the estimated optimal Λ from Proposition 4, nor any measurement of estimator variance or effective sample size. Without these, the unification is demonstrated only as a theory-level observation rather than an empirically verified advantage mechanism.

Computational cost is not analyzed or reported. The proposed estimator requires N samples per (s, t, at) triplet, a backward pass for ∇Q on each sample, and estimation of Λ, which is substantially more expensive than prior objectives. Wall-clock time, gradient steps, and N's sensitivity are all unreported, making it hard to judge the practical trade-off.

No limitations section is present, and key practical failure modes are not discussed: SNIS with unnormalized weights exp(Q/λ) can suffer severe weight collapse when Q-values have large magnitude or the posterior is far from the Gaussian proposal, especially early in training; the t_min trick hints at numerical fragility near t=0 but this is not analyzed.

Several theoretical components are standard or incremental: Lemma 2 is the classical Stein identity, Propositions 4-5 reduce to ordinary linear-regression control variates, and Lemma 3 is a textbook SNIS CLT. Theorem 1's equivalence follows fairly directly because the forward construction's conditional law coincides with the posterior coupling. The novelty lies mainly in assembly rather than in the individual results, and the paper could be more candid about this.

Reproducibility is limited: no hyperparameter tables (N, t_min, λ, learning rates, network sizes), no mention of code release, and experimental details are thin—five seeds over eight relatively modest DMC tasks is a limited evaluation, with no harder benchmarks (e.g., Humanoid, sparse-reward or image-based tasks) where the claimed stability benefits would be most consequential.

The comparison against baselines, while implemented in a common codebase, does not include a flow-policy variant of the prior methods (e.g., a flow version of QNE/DQS), so it is difficult to isolate whether the gains come from the RFM framework/control variates or simply from using a flow policy with a better-tuned objective.

strengths: The unification claim is substantiated rather than merely asserted: Appendix B provides a detailed, step-by-step mapping showing that iDEM/DQS (gradient-expectation, η=1) and QNE/RSM (noise-expectation, η=0) are recovered as special cases of the RFM framework with specific schedules and proposals, which is a genuine contribution to understanding.

Extending Boltzmann-distribution targeting from diffusion to flow policies fills a real gap identified in the literature, and the framework's flexibility (general schedules, general source distributions, reverse score matching in Appendix D) is a natural and useful consequence of the unified derivation.

The control variate construction via Langevin Stein operators is well-motivated: Propositions 4.8-4.10 characterize zero-variance conditions and variance-minimizing coefficients, and the ablations (Figures 4 and 5) directly verify that the adaptive Λ estimator outperforms the fixed η=0 and η=1 variants of prior methods, connecting theory to empirical benefit.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably thorough for an RL paper: eight DeepMind Control Suite environments, five seeds, multiple families of baselines (SAC, QSM, MaxEntDP/QNE, DQS, QVPO), plus extended comparisons with SDAC and DIME, sensitivity analyses over K, M, N, and a training-time comparison (Table 2). RFM appears consistently stable where each baseline fails on at least some tasks.

Reproducibility is aided by a unified JAX codebase, shared hyperparameters (Table 1), a full algorithm pseudocode, explicit SNIS computation details including the ridge-regularized Λ estimator, and ablations on proposal choices (from policy / from buffer / from Gaussian).

Writing is clear and well-structured; the reverse-inferential reframing of flow matching (posterior mean estimation given a noisy interpolant) is pedagogically valuable and the proofs, while not deep, are correct and complete in Appendix C.
weaknesses: There is a theory-practice gap concerning the SNIS estimator. The theoretical results concern exact posterior means, but the implementation uses finite-K SNIS, whose self-normalization introduces bias for finite K. No bias analysis, effective-sample-size diagnostics, or discussion of how this bias propagates through training is provided; K=100 with exponentiated Q weights (λ=0.02) can produce extreme weight distributions, and only a passing mention of a GMM proposal to improve effective sample size appears in Appendix F.

The variance-optimal coefficients in Propositions 4.9-4.10 depend on the unknown posterior mean μ0|t, the very quantity being estimated. The plug-in estimator used in Appendix E is circular (the estimator appears on both sides), and the theoretical guarantee of variance minimization does not strictly apply to the actual plug-in procedure; the additional bias from this step is not analyzed.

Several theoretical results are largely classical or straightforward: the equivalence of the three losses follows from a standard quadratic decomposition (Proposition 4.1), the Stein identity is well-known (Lemma 4.5, Oates et al. 2017), and Propositions 4.9-4.10 are simple quadratic minimizations citing the textbook SNIS CLT (Lemma C.1). The paper's depth lies in assembling these pieces rather than in new mathematics.

Theorem 4.2 guarantees equivalence only of global minimizers under an unrealizable richness assumption; since gradients of LRFM differ from LCFM under any proposal p̂t ≠ pt, nothing is said about the optimization dynamics that actually matter in practice. The empirical finding that p̂t choices perform similarly is presented as consistent with theory, but the theory is silent on this.

An internal inconsistency between framing and implementation: the paper motivates the Boltzmann target via the maximum-entropy/soft policy improvement framework, but the implementation uses a standard (non-soft) Q-function and drops the entropy term, acknowledging this is 'mainly computational.' The soft-Q variant is then empirically inferior, which means the theoretically exact target is not what is optimized; this discrepancy deserves more careful treatment than the current justification.

The empirical scope is limited to continuous-control DeepMind Control Suite tasks; no higher-dimensional or image-based decision-making settings, and no study of sensitivity to the temperature λ (fixed at 0.02 for all environments), which is known to strongly affect exponentiated-Q weighting schemes.

Action selection still relies on generating M=32 candidates and picking the highest-Q action at environment time (inherited from prior works), which is a heuristic layered on top of the policy distribution and complicates the claim that the policy samples from the Boltzmann distribution.

Some results rest on assumptions that are hard to verify in the RL setting (mutual absolute continuity of pt and p̂t, boundary/integrability conditions for the Stein identity with unnormalized targets and tanh-transformed spaces), and the boundary-condition check for the posterior density on R^d is not verified.

strengths: The paper offers a clean and well-motivated unification: it derives the reverse flow matching (RFM) objective via a posterior mean estimation viewpoint and shows explicitly (Appendix B) that the noise-expectation family (QNE/MaxEntDP, SDAC) and the gradient-expectation family (iDEM, DQS) arise as the η=0 and η=1 special cases of one control-variate family. This mapping is worked out carefully, including schedule correspondences (VE/VP), and is a genuine conceptual contribution that clarifies a previously opaque relationship between two method families.

The theoretical development is largely correct and self-contained: Proposition 4.1 (equivalence of the general, noise-posterior, and data-posterior forms up to additive constants) and Theorem 4.2 (same minimizers as CFM under mutual absolute continuity and function-class richness) are proved cleanly in Appendix C. The Langevin Stein operator construction and the zero-variance characterization (Prop. 4.8) give a principled, and slightly novel, way to blend Q-value and Q-gradient information as zero-mean control variates.

The empirical evaluation is more thorough than typical: a 2D toy example with quantitative distribution metrics (SWD, MMD², Sinkhorn), eight DeepMind Control Suite tasks with five seeds, sensitivity analyses over K, M, and N (Fig. 3), ablations on control-variate coefficients, proposal choice p̂_t, and soft-Q usage (Figs. 4-6), extended baselines (SDAC, DIME), training-time comparison, and a unified JAX codebase for fairness. This supports reproducibility.

The principled handling of action bounds via a tanh latent space (including the correct Jacobian factor in the latent-space Boltzmann target) is a useful practical improvement over the truncated-Gaussian heuristics used by prior work, and RFM achieves competitive performance with fewer inference steps (10 flow steps vs. 20 diffusion steps).
weaknesses: Much of the technical machinery is a re-derivation of standard results: the Langevin Stein identity (Lemma 4.5), SNIS asymptotics (Lemma C.1), and the variance-optimal control-variate coefficients (Prop. 4.9/4.10) are classical (Oates et al., 2017; Tokdar & Kass, 2010). The truly new insight—that noise- vs. gradient-expectation families are two endpoints of a control-variate interpolation—is elegant but modest, and the headline framing as a 'unified framework' somewhat oversells it.

The empirical gains are confounded by design choices not isolated in the ablations: the tanh latent-space reparameterization, the selection of M=32 action candidates by max-Q during sampling (which changes the effective behavior policy, not merely Boltzmann sampling), and the learned GMM proposal for SNIS. The ablation section tests proposals p̂_t and control variates, but never quantifies how much of the improvement over DQS/MaxEntDP is attributable to the core RFM objective versus these auxiliary components.

The method as implemented deviates from the maximum-entropy RL theory it cites as motivation: the actor targets a Boltzmann distribution induced by the standard (non-soft) Q-function, and entropy regularization is not enforced. The soft-Q ablation (Fig. 4, right) actually shows the principled variant degrading performance, which the authors attribute to numerical issues in ODE log-likelihood computation. This weakens the claim that RFM 'principledly' instantiates soft policy improvement, and the discrepancy deserves a more careful treatment than a one-line speculation.

Theoretical guarantees concern asymptotic variance and global minimizers under strong assumptions (mutual absolute continuity of p_t and p̂_t, 'sufficiently rich' function class, infinite Monte Carlo samples). There is no finite-sample bias analysis for SNIS with K=100 samples per posterior mean estimate, nor any analysis of how estimator bias compounds over policy improvement iterations. The variance-optimal coefficients (16)-(17) require plug-in estimation of unknown quantities, whose own estimation error is not analyzed.

The claimed benefit of flow models admitting general source distributions (contribution 3) is not exercised: all experiments use a Gaussian source p0 = N(0, I_d), so the 'domain knowledge through tailored source choices' advantage remains speculative. Similarly, the reverse score matching extension (Appendix D) is presented theoretically but not validated empirically.

The benchmark scope is narrow: eight state-based DeepMind Control Suite tasks with modest difficulty, no harder benchmarks (e.g., humanoid, dog, pixel-based observation, AntMaze-style long-horizon tasks), and sample-quality claims rely on a single 2D toy distribution. Figure 2 also shows many baselines overlapping RFM on several tasks, so the 'consistently well across all eight environments' claim, while true for stability, reflects smaller average-return gaps than the framing suggests.

Some claims are under-supported: e.g., 'existing derivations are rigidly coupled with specific noise schedules... obscuring underlying principles' is asserted rather than demonstrated, and the sensitivity analysis is confined to a single environment (walker-run).

strengths: The core idea is clean and well-motivated: instead of forward-sampling (X0, X1) pairs, RFM treats the intermediate X_t as observed evidence and performs reverse inference of the posterior over X_0 (or X_1), converting the intractable problem of 'no target samples from the Boltzmann policy' into a posterior mean estimation problem. This is a genuinely useful reframing for online RL with diffusion/flow policies.

The unification claim is substantiated, not just asserted: Appendix B gives a careful, explicit derivation showing that QNE/RSM (noise-expectation family, η=0) and iDEM/DQS (gradient-expectation family, η=1) are recovered as special cases of the general posterior mean estimator with different test functions. This mapping is valuable for the community and clarifies the relationships among recent methods.

The theoretical results are correct as far as I can verify: Proposition 4.1 and Theorem 4.2 (equivalence of global minimizers under mutual absolute continuity) follow from standard quadratic-decomposition arguments; the Stein operator construction (Lemma 4.5, Props 4.7–4.10) is a competent application of classical Stein identities to build zero-mean control variates, with a sensible variance-optimal coefficient derivation via SNIS asymptotics.

The empirical evaluation is more thorough than typical: 8 DMC tasks with 5 seeds, a unified JAX codebase with shared hyperparameters across baselines, a training-time comparison (Table 2), sensitivity analyses over K, M, N (Figure 3), ablations on control variates, proposal choice, and soft-Q vs Q (Figures 4–6), and extended comparisons with SDAC and DIME (Figure 7). The ablation showing learned Λ outperforms both fixed η=0 and η=1 variants directly supports the claimed practical benefit of the general framework.
The handling of action bounds via a tanh reparameterization with the Jacobian factor included in the weights (Appendix E) is a principled detail often glossed over in diffusion policy papers.
weaknesses: The practical validity of the key theoretical assumption is not established. Theorem 4.2 requires the proposal p̂_t and the true marginal p_t to be mutually absolutely continuous. In the RL algorithm, p̂_t is induced by the current (partially trained) flow policy, and p_t is the marginal of the evolving policy under the Boltzmann target; nothing guarantees shared support during training, especially early on or in high dimensions. The ablations (Figure 4, Figure 6) show robustness to proposal choice empirically, but the gap between the assumption and practice is not analyzed, and there is no discussion of when RFM training could be biased (e.g., zero-weight SNIS degeneracy when p̂_t puts little mass on high-Q regions).

The theoretical novelty is modest in isolation. The Stein identity, SNIS asymptotics (Lemma C.1), and control-variate optimality are all classical; the reverse flow matching objective is a natural twist on conditional flow matching. The paper's value rests substantially on the unification and the empirical gains, so the contribution, while useful, is incremental relative to iDEM/DQS/QNE rather than a new methodological machinery.

The evaluation is confined to a single benchmark suite (DeepMind Control) with relatively simple continuous-control tasks (action dims up to ~6). All claims about 'extending the capability of targeting Boltzmann distributions from diffusion to flow policies' and improved stability rest on these tasks; no higher-dimensional or hierarchical settings, and no report of statistical significance tests (only min–max shading over 5 seeds).

The comparison of inference steps (RFM with 10–20 flow steps vs. baselines with 20–100 diffusion steps) is presented as an advantage, but the fairer comparison is total computation; the training-time table partially addresses this (RFM 15 min vs. QSM 10 min vs. SAC 8 min), yet the per-update cost of K=100 Monte Carlo posterior samples and per-sample Q-gradients is not decomposed, so the efficiency claims are only partially supported.

Several design choices are justified post hoc rather than principled: the temperature is fixed at λ=0.02 across all environments without discussion of sensitivity to λ; the soft-Q ablation is explained by a speculative numerical-instability argument; and the distinction between using Q^π versus T̂πQ in the actor loss (Figure 4, right) is empirically resolved but theoretically unexplored.

Reproducibility is reasonable (hyperparameter table, algorithm box, hardware reported) but no code release is stated, and for a paper whose central contribution is a framework with several estimator variants, released code would be important for others to build on.
